input.rationale: The AddNonvoter control ran (CheckRun 9245773442404356acaafba5198cba2a, exit 0) and did exactly what the discriminator needed: with the same cluster shape, the same merge-and-connect join and the same disconnect of one original voter, only the public join call changed, and the added member came out as a Nonvoter with two voters in the configuration, after which the command did not commit (the future returned leadership lost after about 50 ms and the leader stepped down to Follower), while the new node still received logs. Set against the AddVoter witness in the same shape - member written as Voter, three voters, command committed with one original voter gone - the control shows the disconnect really separates a voting member from a non-voting one, so the witness's inference that the commit required the freshly added member's acknowledgement is not an artefact of some other path. I record the control observation as a fact, record the suffrage difference itself as a behaviour, write the interpretation that closes the residual counterweight on the AddVoter question, and keep the sharp edges: the control confirms the arithmetic, it does not turn the finding into a safety claim, and the mismatch remains a documented-contract defect since the implementation matches its own unit expectations.

investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?
investigations.hypothesis: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet api.go installs processHeartbeat as the transport's heartbeat handler; the network transport classifies a strictly empty AppendEntries request (no previous entry, no entries, no leader commit index) as a heartbeat and dispatches it from its connection goroutine. That request still runs appendEntries' term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat carrying a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine, mutating state the rest of the package treats as owned by the main thread. The in-memory transport used by the test facility explicitly does not support the handler, so the path is unreachable in the harness shapes used so far and the check needs a transport that implements it.
investigations.discriminator: Use a transport that implements the fast path the way the network transport does - forwarding strictly empty AppendEntries requests to the installed handler on the sender's goroutine - occupy the main loop deterministically with the already-validated Restore stall handshake, then deliver one empty heartbeat whose term is above the node's current term and read the node's term and state while the main loop is still inside its handler. A term or leader-state change observed inside that window witnesses off-main-thread mutation; no change, or a change only after the loop resumes, would defeat the suspicion. The prerequisite is deliberate: the in-memory transport no-ops SetHeartbeatHandler, so the harness must supply a transport that fast-paths empty heartbeats rather than relying on the test facility's transport.

knowledge.statement: Whether a command can commit after one member of a three-member configuration becomes unreachable depends on the suffrage the join call wrote: a member added with AddVoter is counted in the leader's quorum arithmetic from the entry that adds it, so a majority of two remains reachable and the command commits, while a member added with AddNonvoter is not counted, no majority remains, and the leader steps down without committing.
knowledge.conditions: Three-member configuration reached by joining a fresh node to a two-voter cluster through the public API, then disconnecting one of the two original voters; observed in this revision with the in-memory transport and the test facility's Disconnect.

interpretations.rationale: The point of this control was to test the one soft spot in the AddVoter account: the witness inferred that the commit after the disconnect required the newly added member's acknowledgement, and an inference about quorum arithmetic is only as good as the discriminator behind it. The control holds the harness fixed and changes only the join call, and the outcome separates the two cases exactly as the arithmetic predicts: with AddNonvoter the member is a Nonvoter, the configuration keeps two voters, and after one original voter is disconnected the command cannot commit - the future returned leadership lost and the leader stepped down - while the added node still advanced its log, which is what a non-voting member is for. With AddVoter in the same shape the member is a Voter, there are three voters, and the same disconnect still leaves a committing majority. So the commit in the witness could not have come from any path other than the added member's acknowledgement, and the earlier counterweight is answered rather than merely acknowledged. That leaves the account of the question where it was, now with both halves witnessed: the public documentation promises a staging member promoted once it is ready, no such state is entered - the member is a voter in the very entry that adds it, in the leader's view and in its own - and the practical difference is exactly the availability arithmetic the documentation's promise would have avoided, since the fresh member counts toward commitment immediately while the control shows what the non-voting case looks like instead. What this does not do is turn the finding into a safety claim: voters still compare logs, so a member that has not caught up cannot win an election, and the implementation still matches its own unit expectations - the defect remains the documented contract that the code never had, not a broken consensus rule.
counterevidence: Both halves are single executions on separate clusters with the test facility's Disconnect rather than a real partition or crash, so the contrast shows the arithmetic as this harness models reachability.

The control's failure mode was leadership loss rather than a silent stall, which is a different shape from the witness's success; the comparison therefore rests on commit versus no commit, not on identical failure timing.

Because the control leaves two voters, it also confirms that a two-voter configuration cannot commit with one member gone, which is standard majority behaviour and not by itself evidence about AddVoter.
limitations: One case and one control, each executed once; the pair establishes that the discriminator works, not a distribution over timings or cluster sizes.
The control used AddNonvoter, which produces a non-voting member by design; it does not exercise the Staging suffrage, which no public path reaches.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the AddVoter witness are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters: MakeCluster(2) merged with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1), fully connected, one elected leader, one original voter disconnected before the apply, and the same bounded apply wait. They differ only in the public join call, AddVoter in the witness and AddNonvoter in the control, so the pair is a same-cause case and control rather than one split history; the control's own receipt is the only one cited here, and the witness receipt is named in the rationale for the contrast.

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. That logFuture has no ShutdownCh, Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and both the main loop and runFSM leave on shutdownCh, so a future left in the buffer has no producer that can respond it: Error() blocks indefinitely and the caller's timeout, which only guarded the enqueue, cannot save it. runLeader's defer responds only futures on leaderState.inflight, so it does not cover a future that was never dispatched. Confirmed by observation: accepted in state Leader, still queued and unresponded after state Shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Occupy the main loop inside a handler (a public Restore with a caller-supplied reader that stalls on its first Read, which is the handshake), accept one Barrier future through the ordinary public path so it lands in the buffered applyCh, then call Shutdown() and observe whether the future is ever responded: a completion would defeat the suspicion and must name the responding producer, while non-completion together with the future still being queued in applyCh shows the duty was accepted and then lost. Executed: no completion; the duty stayed queued with the node in state Shutdown.

knowledge.assertion: the caller's timeout guards only the enqueue, and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so completion is unbounded once the duty is accepted
Shutdown() drains nothing and runLeader's defer covers only leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in applyCh loses its producer

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. Observed twice, on separate clusters with the same harness: target_ever_leader=false, transfer_err empty, term 2 to 4, original leader back in Leader state, and in both runs the target's term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while the recovery election at term 4 ran one.
investigations.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. investigations.question: Does the documented staging phase of AddVoter exist in the implementation: can a server added through the public AddVoter API be a Nonvoter or Staging member that the leader later promotes once it has caught up?
investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The implementation does not have that phase: nextConfiguration builds the AddVoter entry with Suffrage Voter outright, the separate Staging suffrage is only reachable by an explicit Promote command, and the library's own command documentation says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.
investigations.discriminator: Trace every producer of a configuration entry for AddVoter and every consumer of the Staging suffrage: if the only public path that can add a member writes Suffrage Voter and nothing in the non-test code ever issues Promote, the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist, and the mismatch is decidable by reading rather than by execution. Executed by reading: the AddVoter case writes Voter, Promote is only reached by an explicit Promote command that no non-test caller issues, and the unit expectations for AddVoter match the AddStaging cases. An end-to-end witness is queued to confirm the consequence that the added member votes immediately.

The consumer duty is concrete and documented: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry', future.go:27-33), and the documented use of that index is the configuration compare-and-swap: AddVoter and friends describe prevIndex as 'the index of the only configuration upon which this change may be applied; if another configuration entry has been added in the meantime, this request will fail' (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as 'no precondition' (configuration.go:229), so the guard is silently disabled - the request loses the very protection the API promises, and the loss is invisible because the call still succeeds. The same zero is republished as latest_configuration_index in Stats() (api.go:1188), where a constant '0' also misrepresents the node's configuration state to operators. The pending harness (assurance_generated_test.go) is the discriminating observation: it samples the public values next to the main-thread latestIndex on one running bootstrapped leader, which will either confirm the constant zero or defeat the account. Implications are scoped to callers that rely on the index (CAS preconditions, correlating a configuration with a log position); the configuration contents themselves are live and correct, so this is not a consensus-safety defect.
limitations: No execution yet in this turn: the account rests on source reasoning and on the documented API meaning; the harness has been written but has not run, so the observed value is still unknown.
Severity is bounded: callers that ignore Index() are unaffected, and the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved in the direction that supports the defect account, and the decisive operands come from one instance in one execution rather than from a join across scenarios: control_barrier_err is empty (the same Barrier call completed on the undisturbed leader, so acceptance and completion work when a producer exists), freeze_handshake is inside_restore_read (the main loop was inside its own restore handler and could not select on applyCh again), state_at_accept is Leader and duty_accepted is true (the public API handed the caller a future), state_after_shutdown is Shutdown, and the observation reports result=no_completion over a 3000 ms interval with queued_in_apply_ch=1 and apply_ch_capacity=64 - the accepted duty was still sitting in the buffer, with no consumer, after authority was lost. restore_after_release='failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF' shows that the occupied handler was the node's main loop and that it did resume once the reader was released, which also rules out the harness having wedged the node in some other way. The interval is stated as what it is: 3000 ms of non-progress is not by itself the evidence for indefinite blocking; the indefinite part is source-fixed, and it is why the future can never be woken - deferError.Error() waits on the internal error channel alone once respond has not been called (future.go:113-118), and this logFuture is created without a ShutdownCh, unlike the internal restore and snapshot futures that do get one (raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152); Shutdown() only closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown (api.go:1012-1025) while both the main loop and runFSM leave on that channel; and runLeader's defer responds only the futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight (raft.go:502-560), which a duty that never left applyCh is not. The duty was therefore accepted, its basis (a live leader to dispatch it) disappeared, and the accepted obligation was neither cancelled with a reason nor transferred: it was dropped silently, which is exactly the failure the repository's own test file flags for this family at raft_test.go:40-42. The condition that makes it reachable is the documented one: BatchApplyCh decouples acceptance from consumption (config.go:169-174), and the same comment concedes it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply, so a caller that trusts a positive timeout to bound its wait is not protected.

The node was in the middle of an orderly shutdown, so one can argue a shutting-down node owes nothing in flight; the defect account rests on the narrower observation that the API had already accepted the duty and returned a future whose Error() has no shutdown notice and no timeout, leaving the caller unable to distinguish dropped from pending.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved against the harmless reading: the named target never reached Leader, so the transfer did not accomplish what the API call names. The decisive operands from that one execution are target_suffrage=Nonvoter (the target really held no vote, confirmed from the leader's latest configuration), transfer_err empty (the caller was told the transfer was not a failure), target_ever_leader=false with target_state_at_end=Follower, leaders_seen containing only the original leader, and term_before=2 to term_after=4. The impossibility is source-fixed and independent of the window: a server without a vote has no self-vote in electSelf (a vote is cast only when the iterated server's Suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), voters reject its RequestVote after the term adoption that precedes the rejection (raft.go:1664-1684), and a non-voter never starts an election on its own (raft.go:242-250) - so no vote-less member can ever be elected in this revision, and the explicit transfer path accepted one anyway because it only looks for a replication state (raft.go:765-783). The cost side is what the term movement shows: the transfer candidate ran a real election (TimeoutNow sets Candidate and the transfer flag, raft.go:2209-2214, and that flag suppresses pre-vote in the candidate loop, raft.go:294-300), voters adopted the higher term and stepped down before rejecting, and with the term at 4 the sitting leader at term 2 cannot still have been leader, so leadership was lost and had to be re-won. The asymmetry with the implicit path, which deliberately skips non-voters when picking a server (raft.go:2163-2182), shows the explicit input is accepted where the implicit path would have refused it. The report to the caller is the part that turns this from an operator mistake into a defect of the library: the transfer case answers nil when leadership is lost during a transfer because that is the expected outcome (raft.go:734-739), so a caller that named a vote-less server receives the same success signal as a caller whose transfer worked, and cannot tell that authority never reached the named node.

answers.721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-gap-2: No: the named vote-less target never acquired leadership (target_ever_leader=false over the 3 s window, ending in state Follower) while the caller's future reported no error (transfer_err empty), and the cluster's maximum term advanced from 2 to 4 with the original leader in Leader state at the end (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227, parsed event 0). Source shows the negative is structural: a non-voter gets no self-vote and voters reject its request.

counterevidence: This execution contains no same-window control, so the term advance is attributed to the transfer campaign on the source argument that a Leader never campaigns itself and that a voter adopts a higher term before rejecting it; the control just queued (same path, voter target) separates 'the mechanism does not work here' from 'the mechanism works and a vote-less target cannot take the leadership', but it does not by itself exclude spontaneous election noise in a 3 s window.

The end state is the same as the start (the original leader leads again), so a caller that inspects only who leads afterwards sees no damage; the observed harm is the term movement and the inferred loss of leadership in between, not a lasting loss.

The target's vote was removed by the caller's own previous API call in the same run, so this is not a case where the library silently mis-states an operator-managed configuration; the operator asked for the demotion, then asked for a transfer to the demoted node.
limitations: Single execution and a single target; the claim that a vote-less member can never win rests on the election code paths above, not on repeated runs.

The caller's success value is explained by the lost-leadership branch (raft.go:734-739); the same CheckRun's DEBUG log names that branch ('lost leadership during transfer (expected)'), which corroborates the reading but is the library's own message text rather than an independent probe of the returned value.

The intermediate sequence is observed in the run's own log rather than merely inferred: at 16:26:25.836 the target enters candidate state at term=3 with no pre-vote success line and asks all three voters for a vote while never logging a self-vote, each voter logs term adoption ('lost leadership because received a requestVote with a newer term') immediately followed by 'rejecting vote request since node is not a voter: from=927e473c...', and at 16:26:25.894 the original leader campaigns at term=4 (pre-vote tally 2 of votesNeeded 2) and re-enters leader state; these are the library's own log messages, while the sampled CA_EVENT operands remain the states, term endpoints and window.

Because the term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while both genuine elections in the same run recorded a successful pre-vote first, the log also distinguishes the transfer path from an ordinary election; what it does not provide is a run of the same window without the transfer call, which is why the control case is queued rather than assumed.

interpretations.rationale: The control predicate was that the same call with a voter as the named target does move leadership to that server, and it holds: the target was the only leader observed, ended in Leader state, the original leader ended in Follower and never led again, and the term moved 2 to 3, a single step. That matters twice over for the question about vote-less targets. First, it removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness, because the identical call delivered leadership when the target had a vote; combined with the source facts that a non-voter casts no self-vote (a vote is cast only for servers whose suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), that voters reject its RequestVote after adopting its higher term (raft.go:1664-1684), and that a non-voter never starts an election by itself (raft.go:242-250), the failure to transfer is attributable to the target's lacking a vote rather than to the harness or to the call. Second, it makes the cost of the vote-less attempt visible relative to the intended path: the successful transfer advanced the term by one and placed the named server in charge, while the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the campaign at term 3 and the re-election at term 4 seen in that run's log) and left the same server as a follower, so the request consumed an extra election and returned no benefit. It also corrects my earlier emphasis: transfer_err was empty in both cases, so the empty error is not what marks the failure - in the control it accompanies success. The discriminating evidence is the pair of outcomes (target_ever_leader true with one term step, versus false with two term steps) plus the two source arguments, and the caller-visible gap remains that both callers receive the same success signal while only one of them had authority moved to the named node. The current account is therefore unchanged in substance and better bounded: the defect is that the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership and reports success, and I keep the residual uncertainty about timing variation rather than smoothing it away, which is what the queued repeat of the vote-less case examines.
counterevidence: The two cases are separate executions on separate clusters, not a randomized paired trial, so run-to-run timing variation is not excluded by the pair alone; what the pair excludes is the specific alternative that the transfer mechanism does not work in this harness, and the queued repeat tests whether the vote-less non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur.
An empty transfer error occurs in both cases, so it cannot be used as the distinguishing signal; the earlier account leaned on that value and is narrowed here to the outcome and term-cost operands.

In the control the original leader ended as a follower without leading again, while in the vote-less case leadership stayed with the original server; a caller watching only the final leader could therefore see the vote-less request as harmless, and the harm is the wasted election cycle rather than a lasting loss.
limitations: Each case is a single execution with a single target chosen among followers; neither case repeats a target of the other suffrage type more than once, so the comparison rests on two runs plus the source paths.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

The vote-less case's target had been demoted by the caller in the same run, so the configuration change and the transfer are not separated in time in that execution; the control has no such change, which is a second difference between the two runs besides suffrage.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the vote-less case are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters of the same shape (MakeCluster(4) with default config, one elected leader, a follower chosen from Follower state as target, 3 s sampling every 20 ms). They differ in exactly one input: in the vote-less case the target is first demoted by a committed DemoteVoter, in the control it keeps its vote. They are independent executions rather than one split history, so the pair supports a same-cause comparison (transition works with a vote, does not deliver without one) and does not by itself exclude run-to-run timing variation.

interpretations.rationale: This run was queued to test the one gap I had left explicit, that the earlier vote-less result might have been a timing accident rather than the mechanism. The reproduction is exact on every operand: target_suffrage=Nonvoter, transfer_err empty, target_ever_leader=false with the target ending as Follower, the original leader the only server seen leading and in Leader state at the end, and the term advancing 2 to 4 - the same two-step cost as the first run, against a single step for the voter-target control. The second run's log repeats the internal sequence as well: the target enters candidate state at term 3 with no pre-vote lines of its own while both genuine elections in that run record pre-voting for self and a pre-vote success, each voter logs adopting the higher term immediately before rejecting a node that is not a voter, and the recovery election at term 4 is a real pre-voted election won by the original server with tally 2 of votesNeeded 2. That is the mechanism the sources predict - a candidate that holds no vote gets no self-vote, cannot be granted one by voters, and yet moves the term it runs at, so the caller spends an election and receives no transfer - and it now holds for two independent executions. What the repeat does not buy is a broader sample: both runs use the same fixed harness, the same cluster size and the same sequence of caller steps, so this is schedule variation on one scenario, and I keep that as the boundary of the claim rather than treating two runs as generality. The defect account for the question is unchanged and now reproducible: the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership, moves no authority to it, and reports the same success value it reports when a real transfer succeeds (the control also reported an empty error), so the caller cannot distinguish a transfer that happened from one that never could.
counterevidence: Both runs come from the same fixed harness with the same inputs, so the repetition tests scheduling variation of one scenario rather than a range of cluster sizes, timings or target choices; the source argument for the impossibility of a vote-less winner is what covers those unobserved variants.

As in the earlier control, an empty transfer error accompanies both the successful and the unsuccessful case, so the empty value is not evidence of failure by itself and the account rests on the outcome and term-cost operands.
The demotion that makes the target vote-less is performed by the caller in the same run, so the run does not separate the configuration change from the transfer in time.
limitations: Two runs, one scenario: the reproduction is exact but narrow, and the claim that a vote-less member can never win still rests on the election code paths rather than on sampling many configurations.

The term cost is compared as an endpoint-to-endpoint difference between runs; the intermediate steps are corroborated by the library's own log messages, not by an independent probe of the term value at each instant.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was that the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist if the only public path that adds a member writes Voter and nothing issues Promote, and reading settles it. The public path is api.go's AddVoter (api.go:946-957), which builds an AddVoter change request; the leader turns that into a configuration entry through nextConfiguration, whose AddVoter case constructs the new server with Suffrage Voter and either replaces the existing entry or appends it (configuration.go:234-255), so the member becomes a voting member in the same entry that introduces it. Staging is a distinct suffrage that only the Promote case leaves (configuration.go:291-297), and no non-test code issues Promote, so the state the documentation describes is unreachable from the public API and the 'promote once ready' duty it promises is owed by nobody. The library itself resolves the contradiction about which side is intended: its command table says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it (configuration.go:101-107), and the unit expectations assert the implemented behavior for AddVoter - a Voter when the member was missing, Staging or Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:185-193) - mirroring the AddStaging cases exactly. The documentation therefore describes a contract the code never had, and a consumer that plans around it is wrong about a safety-adjacent property: contrary to the documented staging phase and the membership note that new servers are caught up before being granted a vote, a member added this way counts in elections and in the leader's quorum from the moment the entry exists. What this claim does not say is that the code is wrong: consensus safety is not broken by it, because the log-comparison rule still keeps a less up-to-date candidate from winning, and the implementation matches its own tests. The defect is the promise in the public documentation, and its practical weight is availability planning rather than safety - quorum arithmetic changes at once, and a member far behind the leader is counted in the commitment quorum while the documented design would not have counted it.
counterevidence: The doc comment is prose, not a test-enforced guarantee, and membership.md is a historical design proposal rather than a contract; a reviewer may reasonably read this as stale documentation to be fixed rather than as a violated requirement.
The unit expectations assert the implemented behavior, so the implementation is deliberate; nothing in the snapshot suggests a partial rollout or a disabled staging path.
Consensus safety is unaffected: a member that has not caught up cannot win an election because voters compare logs, so the mismatch costs availability reasoning rather than correctness.

The documentation does promise a protection, so the account would be defeated if some other public path produced a non-voting member first and promoted it later; no such path was found in the non-test code.
limitations: No execution for this question yet: the account rests on the code, the command table, the doc comment and the unit expectations, and the concrete end-to-end consequence is what the queued witness examines.
This is a documentation-contract finding: it is decidable by reading, and its severity depends on how the maintainers rank the doc comment against the implemented, tested behavior.

interpretations.rationale: The source reading said the documented staging phase does not exist because the only public path that adds a member writes a voter and nothing issues Promote; the execution now shows the consequence on a real cluster rather than only the mechanism. The join itself succeeded through the public API (add_err empty, index 3), and the member is a voter in both views - the leader's latest configuration and the new node's own configuration each report suffrage Voter, with three voters in the configuration - so the state the documentation describes is not merely unreachable in source, it is absent after the call that the documentation describes. The decisive availability operand is the apply after one original voter was disconnected: it committed, and with three voters of which one of the original two was unreachable, the majority of two cannot be assembled without the newly added member's acknowledgement, so the commit shows the fresh member counted in the leader's quorum. The documentation's promise is the opposite of that: api.go's AddVoter comment says the server is added as a staging server and promoted by the leader once it is ready, and membership.md lists catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a goal, while the command table and the unit expectations show the library intends and tests the immediate-voter behaviour. So the defect is the documented contract, not the implementation: a caller who plans around the documented staging protection has a member counting in elections and in the commitment quorum immediately, and the promotion duty the doc mentions is owed by nobody. The scope stays narrow and I keep it that way: no consensus-safety rule is broken, because a member whose log is behind cannot win an election, and the cost is availability arithmetic and caller expectations. The control I queued is what keeps this honest, since the commit could in principle have come from a path other than the new member; if the same harness with AddNonvoter also commits after the disconnect, the discriminator is wrong and this account would need rework.
counterevidence: The commit after the disconnect is an inference about which acknowledgement satisfied the quorum: it follows from the configuration arithmetic (three voters, one unreachable, majority two) rather than from a per-server match-index trace, which is why the AddNonvoter control is queued rather than assumed.

The doc comment is prose and membership.md is a design proposal, so a reviewer may treat this as stale documentation to be corrected rather than a violated requirement; the implementation matches its unit expectations.
Consensus safety is unaffected: voters compare logs, so a member that has not caught up cannot win an election.
The disconnect was done through the test facility rather than by a real crash or partition, so the operand shows reachability as the harness models it.
limitations: One cluster and one execution: the witness is a single join with a single disconnect, and the control is queued rather than already run.
The measured effect is about when the member counts, not about whether it caught up; the new node's last index after the run is recorded but no intermediate replication timeline was sampled.

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

result.summary: The AddNonvoter control ran (CheckRun 9245773442404356acaafba5198cba2a, exit 0) and validated the discriminator behind the AddVoter witness. With the harness held fixed and only the public join call changed, the added member came out as a Nonvoter with two voters in the configuration, and after one original voter was disconnected the next command did not commit - the future returned leadership lost after about 50 ms and the leader stepped down to Follower - while the added node still advanced its log. Against the witness, where the member was written as a Voter, three voters were present, and the same disconnect still left a committing majority, the pair shows the commit in the witness could only have come from the freshly added member's acknowledgement, so the earlier counterweight is answered rather than merely noted. I recorded the control observation as a fact and the suffrage-decides-commit contrast as a behaviour citing both receipts, and wrote the interpretation that closes that residual uncertainty while keeping the edges sharp: this is a documented-contract defect, because the implementation matches its own unit expectations, and no consensus-safety rule is broken since voters still compare logs before granting votes. I also opened one new sourced question for the remaining budget: raft.go marks processHeartbeat and appendEntries as main-thread-only, yet the network transport will dispatch a strictly empty AppendEntries request to that handler from its connection goroutine, and such a request still runs the term logic, so a heartbeat carrying a higher term can call setState and setCurrentTerm off the main thread. The question is recorded with the discovery that the in-memory transport no-ops SetHeartbeatHandler - so this path is unreachable in every harness shape used so far - and with a discriminator that requires a transport implementing the fast path for real; I assert no defect claim on it yet, and the earlier witnessed findings on the configuration index, duties lost at shutdown, and the vote-less transfer all remain recorded and unaffected.

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?

investigations.question: Does the transport heartbeat fast path run appendEntries outside the main thread, and can that be observed as a term or leader-state change while the main loop is provably occupied?

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved in the direction that supports the defect account, and the decisive operands come from one instance in one execution rather than from a join across scenarios: control_barrier_err is empty (the same Barrier call completed on the undisturbed leader, so acceptance and completion work when a producer exists), freeze_handshake is inside_restore_read (the main loop was inside its own restore handler and could not select on applyCh again), state_at_accept is Leader and duty_accepted is true (the public API handed the caller a future), state_after_shutdown is Shutdown, and the observation reports result=no_completion over a 3000 ms interval with queued_in_apply_ch=1 and apply_ch_capacity=64 - the accepted duty was still sitting in the buffer, with no consumer, after authority was lost. restore_after_release='failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF' shows that the occupied handler was the node's main loop and that it did resume once the reader was released, which also rules out the harness having wedged the node in some other way. The interval is stated as what it is: 3000 ms of non-progress is not by itself the evidence for indefinite blocking; the indefinite part is source-fixed, and it is why the future can never be woken - deferError.Error() waits on the internal error channel alone once respond has not been called (future.go:113-118), and this logFuture is created without a ShutdownCh, unlike the internal restore and snapshot futures that do get one (raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152); Shutdown() only closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown (api.go:1012-1025) while both the main loop and runFSM leave on that channel; and runLeader's defer responds only the futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight (raft.go:502-560), which a duty that never left applyCh is not. The duty was therefore accepted, its basis (a live leader to dispatch it) disappeared, and the accepted obligation was neither cancelled with a reason nor transferred: it was dropped silently, which is exactly the failure the repository's own test file flags for this family at raft_test.go:40-42. The condition that makes it reachable is the documented one: BatchApplyCh decouples acceptance from consumption (config.go:169-174), and the same comment concedes it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply, so a caller that trusts a positive timeout to bound its wait is not protected.

answers.f2c2b4e0415449d4941c8e53ffbc722e-gap-1: No producer responded the accepted Barrier future after Shutdown(), and the duty was still queued at that point: with the leader occupied inside its own Restore handler, the Barrier future was accepted in state Leader and, after Shutdown() moved the node to state Shutdown, the future had not been responded within the 3000 ms observation while len(applyCh)=1 of capacity 64 (CheckRun c5d127c955b549a8888fe6bab568dbce, parsed event 0).

knowledge.assertion: the timeout guards only the enqueue into applyCh and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so no timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion follows acceptance
Shutdown() leaves applyCh undrained and runLeader's defer responds only leaderState.inflight futures, so the queued duty has no remaining producer

counterevidence: The reachable window needs the main loop to be occupied at the moment of acceptance and shutdown; the harness makes that deterministic with a caller-supplied reader that stalls, so the execution shows the mechanism, not a frequency of occurrence under spontaneous timing.

The window also needs BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174); with the default unbuffered applyCh the enqueue itself is the handoff, so the same duty would instead be rejected at enqueue via the caller's timeout or shutdownCh escape in Apply.

The node was in the middle of an orderly shutdown, so one can argue a shutting-down node owes nothing in flight; the defect account rests on the narrower observation that the API had already accepted the duty and returned a future whose Error() has no shutdown notice and no timeout, leaving the caller unable to distinguish dropped from pending.
limitations: Single node and single execution; the claim that no completion path remains rests on the source argument above (no writer to the error channel after shutdown; every completer exits on shutdownCh), not on repeated sampling or on an unbounded wait.

Only the Barrier path was executed. VerifyLeader constructs its verifyFuture without a ShutdownCh too and sends it on a 64-buffered channel (api.go:883-893, api.go:568), so it shares the shape, but that is a source-level observation and was not exercised.
The scenario models a slow caller-supplied stream keeping the handler busy; it does not claim that shutdown always finds a duty in the buffer.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved against the harmless reading: the named target never reached Leader, so the transfer did not accomplish what the API call names. The decisive operands from that one execution are target_suffrage=Nonvoter (the target really held no vote, confirmed from the leader's latest configuration), transfer_err empty (the caller was told the transfer was not a failure), target_ever_leader=false with target_state_at_end=Follower, leaders_seen containing only the original leader, and term_before=2 to term_after=4. The impossibility is source-fixed and independent of the window: a server without a vote has no self-vote in electSelf (a vote is cast only when the iterated server's Suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), voters reject its RequestVote after the term adoption that precedes the rejection (raft.go:1664-1684), and a non-voter never starts an election on its own (raft.go:242-250) - so no vote-less member can ever be elected in this revision, and the explicit transfer path accepted one anyway because it only looks for a replication state (raft.go:765-783). The cost side is what the term movement shows: the transfer candidate ran a real election (TimeoutNow sets Candidate and the transfer flag, raft.go:2209-2214, and that flag suppresses pre-vote in the candidate loop, raft.go:294-300), voters adopted the higher term and stepped down before rejecting, and with the term at 4 the sitting leader at term 2 cannot still have been leader, so leadership was lost and had to be re-won. The asymmetry with the implicit path, which deliberately skips non-voters when picking a server (raft.go:2163-2182), shows the explicit input is accepted where the implicit path would have refused it. The report to the caller is the part that turns this from an operator mistake into a defect of the library: the transfer case answers nil when leadership is lost during a transfer because that is the expected outcome (raft.go:734-739), so a caller that named a vote-less server receives the same success signal as a caller whose transfer worked, and cannot tell that authority never reached the named node.

answers.721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-gap-2: No: the named vote-less target never acquired leadership (target_ever_leader=false over the 3 s window, ending in state Follower) while the caller's future reported no error (transfer_err empty), and the cluster's maximum term advanced from 2 to 4 with the original leader in Leader state at the end (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227, parsed event 0). Source shows the negative is structural: a non-voter gets no self-vote and voters reject its request.

counterevidence: This execution contains no same-window control, so the term advance is attributed to the transfer campaign on the source argument that a Leader never campaigns itself and that a voter adopts a higher term before rejecting it; the control just queued (same path, voter target) separates 'the mechanism does not work here' from 'the mechanism works and a vote-less target cannot take the leadership', but it does not by itself exclude spontaneous election noise in a 3 s window.

The end state is the same as the start (the original leader leads again), so a caller that inspects only who leads afterwards sees no damage; the observed harm is the term movement and the inferred loss of leadership in between, not a lasting loss.

The target's vote was removed by the caller's own previous API call in the same run, so this is not a case where the library silently mis-states an operator-managed configuration; the operator asked for the demotion, then asked for a transfer to the demoted node.
limitations: Single execution and a single target; the claim that a vote-less member can never win rests on the election code paths above, not on repeated runs.

The caller's success value is explained by the lost-leadership branch (raft.go:734-739); the same CheckRun's DEBUG log names that branch ('lost leadership during transfer (expected)'), which corroborates the reading but is the library's own message text rather than an independent probe of the returned value.

The intermediate sequence is observed in the run's own log rather than merely inferred: at 16:26:25.836 the target enters candidate state at term=3 with no pre-vote success line and asks all three voters for a vote while never logging a self-vote, each voter logs term adoption ('lost leadership because received a requestVote with a newer term') immediately followed by 'rejecting vote request since node is not a voter: from=927e473c...', and at 16:26:25.894 the original leader campaigns at term=4 (pre-vote tally 2 of votesNeeded 2) and re-enters leader state; these are the library's own log messages, while the sampled CA_EVENT operands remain the states, term endpoints and window.

Because the term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while both genuine elections in the same run recorded a successful pre-vote first, the log also distinguishes the transfer path from an ordinary election; what it does not provide is a run of the same window without the transfer call, which is why the control case is queued rather than assumed.

interpretations.rationale: The control predicate was that the same call with a voter as the named target does move leadership to that server, and it holds: the target was the only leader observed, ended in Leader state, the original leader ended in Follower and never led again, and the term moved 2 to 3, a single step. That matters twice over for the question about vote-less targets. First, it removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness, because the identical call delivered leadership when the target had a vote; combined with the source facts that a non-voter casts no self-vote (a vote is cast only for servers whose suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), that voters reject its RequestVote after adopting its higher term (raft.go:1664-1684), and that a non-voter never starts an election by itself (raft.go:242-250), the failure to transfer is attributable to the target's lacking a vote rather than to the harness or to the call. Second, it makes the cost of the vote-less attempt visible relative to the intended path: the successful transfer advanced the term by one and placed the named server in charge, while the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the campaign at term 3 and the re-election at term 4 seen in that run's log) and left the same server as a follower, so the request consumed an extra election and returned no benefit. It also corrects my earlier emphasis: transfer_err was empty in both cases, so the empty error is not what marks the failure - in the control it accompanies success. The discriminating evidence is the pair of outcomes (target_ever_leader true with one term step, versus false with two term steps) plus the two source arguments, and the caller-visible gap remains that both callers receive the same success signal while only one of them had authority moved to the named node. The current account is therefore unchanged in substance and better bounded: the defect is that the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership and reports success, and I keep the residual uncertainty about timing variation rather than smoothing it away, which is what the queued repeat of the vote-less case examines.
counterevidence: The two cases are separate executions on separate clusters, not a randomized paired trial, so run-to-run timing variation is not excluded by the pair alone; what the pair excludes is the specific alternative that the transfer mechanism does not work in this harness, and the queued repeat tests whether the vote-less non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur.
An empty transfer error occurs in both cases, so it cannot be used as the distinguishing signal; the earlier account leaned on that value and is narrowed here to the outcome and term-cost operands.

In the control the original leader ended as a follower without leading again, while in the vote-less case leadership stayed with the original server; a caller watching only the final leader could therefore see the vote-less request as harmless, and the harm is the wasted election cycle rather than a lasting loss.
limitations: Each case is a single execution with a single target chosen among followers; neither case repeats a target of the other suffrage type more than once, so the comparison rests on two runs plus the source paths.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

The vote-less case's target had been demoted by the caller in the same run, so the configuration change and the transfer are not separated in time in that execution; the control has no such change, which is a second difference between the two runs besides suffrage.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the vote-less case are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters of the same shape (MakeCluster(4) with default config, one elected leader, a follower chosen from Follower state as target, 3 s sampling every 20 ms). They differ in exactly one input: in the vote-less case the target is first demoted by a committed DemoteVoter, in the control it keeps its vote. They are independent executions rather than one split history, so the pair supports a same-cause comparison (transition works with a vote, does not deliver without one) and does not by itself exclude run-to-run timing variation.

interpretations.rationale: This run was queued to test the one gap I had left explicit, that the earlier vote-less result might have been a timing accident rather than the mechanism. The reproduction is exact on every operand: target_suffrage=Nonvoter, transfer_err empty, target_ever_leader=false with the target ending as Follower, the original leader the only server seen leading and in Leader state at the end, and the term advancing 2 to 4 - the same two-step cost as the first run, against a single step for the voter-target control. The second run's log repeats the internal sequence as well: the target enters candidate state at term 3 with no pre-vote lines of its own while both genuine elections in that run record pre-voting for self and a pre-vote success, each voter logs adopting the higher term immediately before rejecting a node that is not a voter, and the recovery election at term 4 is a real pre-voted election won by the original server with tally 2 of votesNeeded 2. That is the mechanism the sources predict - a candidate that holds no vote gets no self-vote, cannot be granted one by voters, and yet moves the term it runs at, so the caller spends an election and receives no transfer - and it now holds for two independent executions. What the repeat does not buy is a broader sample: both runs use the same fixed harness, the same cluster size and the same sequence of caller steps, so this is schedule variation on one scenario, and I keep that as the boundary of the claim rather than treating two runs as generality. The defect account for the question is unchanged and now reproducible: the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership, moves no authority to it, and reports the same success value it reports when a real transfer succeeds (the control also reported an empty error), so the caller cannot distinguish a transfer that happened from one that never could.
counterevidence: Both runs come from the same fixed harness with the same inputs, so the repetition tests scheduling variation of one scenario rather than a range of cluster sizes, timings or target choices; the source argument for the impossibility of a vote-less winner is what covers those unobserved variants.

As in the earlier control, an empty transfer error accompanies both the successful and the unsuccessful case, so the empty value is not evidence of failure by itself and the account rests on the outcome and term-cost operands.
The demotion that makes the target vote-less is performed by the caller in the same run, so the run does not separate the configuration change from the transfer in time.
limitations: Two runs, one scenario: the reproduction is exact but narrow, and the claim that a vote-less member can never win still rests on the election code paths rather than on sampling many configurations.

The term cost is compared as an endpoint-to-endpoint difference between runs; the intermediate steps are corroborated by the library's own log messages, not by an independent probe of the term value at each instant.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was that the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist if the only public path that adds a member writes Voter and nothing issues Promote, and reading settles it. The public path is api.go's AddVoter (api.go:946-957), which builds an AddVoter change request; the leader turns that into a configuration entry through nextConfiguration, whose AddVoter case constructs the new server with Suffrage Voter and either replaces the existing entry or appends it (configuration.go:234-255), so the member becomes a voting member in the same entry that introduces it. Staging is a distinct suffrage that only the Promote case leaves (configuration.go:291-297), and no non-test code issues Promote, so the state the documentation describes is unreachable from the public API and the 'promote once ready' duty it promises is owed by nobody. The library itself resolves the contradiction about which side is intended: its command table says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it (configuration.go:101-107), and the unit expectations assert the implemented behavior for AddVoter - a Voter when the member was missing, Staging or Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:185-193) - mirroring the AddStaging cases exactly. The documentation therefore describes a contract the code never had, and a consumer that plans around it is wrong about a safety-adjacent property: contrary to the documented staging phase and the membership note that new servers are caught up before being granted a vote, a member added this way counts in elections and in the leader's quorum from the moment the entry exists. What this claim does not say is that the code is wrong: consensus safety is not broken by it, because the log-comparison rule still keeps a less up-to-date candidate from winning, and the implementation matches its own tests. The defect is the promise in the public documentation, and its practical weight is availability planning rather than safety - quorum arithmetic changes at once, and a member far behind the leader is counted in the commitment quorum while the documented design would not have counted it.
counterevidence: The doc comment is prose, not a test-enforced guarantee, and membership.md is a historical design proposal rather than a contract; a reviewer may reasonably read this as stale documentation to be fixed rather than as a violated requirement.
The unit expectations assert the implemented behavior, so the implementation is deliberate; nothing in the snapshot suggests a partial rollout or a disabled staging path.
Consensus safety is unaffected: a member that has not caught up cannot win an election because voters compare logs, so the mismatch costs availability reasoning rather than correctness.

The documentation does promise a protection, so the account would be defeated if some other public path produced a non-voting member first and promoted it later; no such path was found in the non-test code.
limitations: No execution for this question yet: the account rests on the code, the command table, the doc comment and the unit expectations, and the concrete end-to-end consequence is what the queued witness examines.
This is a documentation-contract finding: it is decidable by reading, and its severity depends on how the maintainers rank the doc comment against the implemented, tested behavior.

interpretations.rationale: The source reading said the documented staging phase does not exist because the only public path that adds a member writes a voter and nothing issues Promote; the execution now shows the consequence on a real cluster rather than only the mechanism. The join itself succeeded through the public API (add_err empty, index 3), and the member is a voter in both views - the leader's latest configuration and the new node's own configuration each report suffrage Voter, with three voters in the configuration - so the state the documentation describes is not merely unreachable in source, it is absent after the call that the documentation describes. The decisive availability operand is the apply after one original voter was disconnected: it committed, and with three voters of which one of the original two was unreachable, the majority of two cannot be assembled without the newly added member's acknowledgement, so the commit shows the fresh member counted in the leader's quorum. The documentation's promise is the opposite of that: api.go's AddVoter comment says the server is added as a staging server and promoted by the leader once it is ready, and membership.md lists catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a goal, while the command table and the unit expectations show the library intends and tests the immediate-voter behaviour. So the defect is the documented contract, not the implementation: a caller who plans around the documented staging protection has a member counting in elections and in the commitment quorum immediately, and the promotion duty the doc mentions is owed by nobody. The scope stays narrow and I keep it that way: no consensus-safety rule is broken, because a member whose log is behind cannot win an election, and the cost is availability arithmetic and caller expectations. The control I queued is what keeps this honest, since the commit could in principle have come from a path other than the new member; if the same harness with AddNonvoter also commits after the disconnect, the discriminator is wrong and this account would need rework.
counterevidence: The commit after the disconnect is an inference about which acknowledgement satisfied the quorum: it follows from the configuration arithmetic (three voters, one unreachable, majority two) rather than from a per-server match-index trace, which is why the AddNonvoter control is queued rather than assumed.

The doc comment is prose and membership.md is a design proposal, so a reviewer may treat this as stale documentation to be corrected rather than a violated requirement; the implementation matches its unit expectations.
Consensus safety is unaffected: voters compare logs, so a member that has not caught up cannot win an election.
The disconnect was done through the test facility rather than by a real crash or partition, so the operand shows reachability as the harness models it.
limitations: One cluster and one execution: the witness is a single join with a single disconnect, and the control is queued rather than already run.
The measured effect is about when the member counts, not about whether it caught up; the new node's last index after the run is recorded but no intermediate replication timeline was sampled.

interpretations.rationale: The point of this control was to test the one soft spot in the AddVoter account: the witness inferred that the commit after the disconnect required the newly added member's acknowledgement, and an inference about quorum arithmetic is only as good as the discriminator behind it. The control holds the harness fixed and changes only the join call, and the outcome separates the two cases exactly as the arithmetic predicts: with AddNonvoter the member is a Nonvoter, the configuration keeps two voters, and after one original voter is disconnected the command cannot commit - the future returned leadership lost and the leader stepped down - while the added node still advanced its log, which is what a non-voting member is for. With AddVoter in the same shape the member is a Voter, there are three voters, and the same disconnect still leaves a committing majority. So the commit in the witness could not have come from any path other than the added member's acknowledgement, and the earlier counterweight is answered rather than merely acknowledged. That leaves the account of the question where it was, now with both halves witnessed: the public documentation promises a staging member promoted once it is ready, no such state is entered - the member is a voter in the very entry that adds it, in the leader's view and in its own - and the practical difference is exactly the availability arithmetic the documentation's promise would have avoided, since the fresh member counts toward commitment immediately while the control shows what the non-voting case looks like instead. What this does not do is turn the finding into a safety claim: voters still compare logs, so a member that has not caught up cannot win an election, and the implementation still matches its own unit expectations - the defect remains the documented contract that the code never had, not a broken consensus rule.
counterevidence: Both halves are single executions on separate clusters with the test facility's Disconnect rather than a real partition or crash, so the contrast shows the arithmetic as this harness models reachability.

The control's failure mode was leadership loss rather than a silent stall, which is a different shape from the witness's success; the comparison therefore rests on commit versus no commit, not on identical failure timing.

Because the control leaves two voters, it also confirms that a two-voter configuration cannot commit with one member gone, which is standard majority behaviour and not by itself evidence about AddVoter.
limitations: One case and one control, each executed once; the pair establishes that the discriminator works, not a distribution over timings or cluster sizes.
The control used AddNonvoter, which produces a non-voting member by design; it does not exercise the Staging suffrage, which no public path reaches.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the AddVoter witness are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters: MakeCluster(2) merged with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1), fully connected, one elected leader, one original voter disconnected before the apply, and the same bounded apply wait. They differ only in the public join call, AddVoter in the witness and AddNonvoter in the control, so the pair is a same-cause case and control rather than one split history; the control's own receipt is the only one cited here, and the witness receipt is named in the rationale for the contrast.

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.
